title: 22. Interview: GraphQL
summary: Interview Q&A for GraphQL — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 GraphQL interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What problem does GraphQL solve that REST does not?
**Answer:** GraphQL solves two problems that REST suffers from: **over-fetching** and **under-fetching**. Over-fetching: a REST endpoint returns a fixed shape — `GET /users/42` returns `{id, name, email, phone, address, bio, ...}` even if the client only needs `name` and `avatar_url`. Under-fetching: rendering a single page may require REST calls to `/users/42`, `/users/42/posts`, `/users/42/followers`, `/users/42/settings` — 4 round-trips on a mobile network. GraphQL lets the client send a single query to one endpoint (`POST /graphql`) specifying exactly the fields it needs, and the server returns a JSON object matching that shape. One round-trip, no over-fetching. This was Facebook's original motivation: rendering News Feed on a 3G phone required stitching together 6–10 REST calls, each over-fetching fields the phone did not need. By 2017 GitHub shipped GraphQL API v4 because REST v3 was forcing 5–10 round-trips to render a single repository's issue list. Shopify made their storefront API GraphQL-only because mobile commerce clients benefit most. Trade-off: GraphQL shifts complexity from the client to the server, which now must parse, validate, and resolve queries against a schema.
**Visual:**
```
REST (over-fetching + under-fetching):
   GET /users/42            -> {id,name,email,phone,address,bio,...}  (over-fetch)
   GET /users/42/posts      -> [...]
   GET /users/42/followers  -> [...]
   (3 round-trips)

GraphQL (exact shape, 1 round-trip):
   POST /graphql
   { user(id:42){ name posts{title} followers{name} } }
   -> { "data": { "name": "Ada", "posts": [...], "followers": [...] } }
```

### Q2. What are queries, mutations, and subscriptions in GraphQL?
**Answer:** Three root operations. **Query** is a read — analogous to REST GET; the spec allows queries to execute in parallel for performance. Example: `query { user(id:42){ name posts{ title } } }`. **Mutation** is a write — analogous to REST POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE; the spec requires mutations to execute sequentially (top-level fields in order) so side effects are predictable. Example: `mutation { createUser(input:{name:"Ada"}){ id name } }`. **Subscription** is a long-lived stream — the client opens a WebSocket (or SSE) connection and sends a subscription; the server pushes updates whenever the underlying data changes. Example: `subscription { commentAdded(postId:42){ id body author{name} } }` — every time someone comments on post 42, the server pushes the new comment to all subscribers. Subscriptions are how real-time apps are built on top of GraphQL — chat apps, live dashboards, collaborative editors. The trade-offs: queries are easy to cache (via persisted queries and Apollo's normalized cache); mutations are not cacheable but benefit from idempotency keys (same as REST); subscriptions are the most operationally complex because they require persistent WebSocket connections, sticky load balancing (the same client must keep hitting the same server to receive its subscriptions), and careful backpressure handling. GitHub, Shopify, and Netflix all use subscriptions for real-time features (live issue updates, order status, studio notifications).
**Visual:**
```
Query:        query { user(id:42){ name } }              -> read, parallel
Mutation:     mutation { createUser(input){ id } }        -> write, sequential
Subscription: subscription { commentAdded(postId:42){    -> stream over WebSocket
                                  id body author{ name } } }
                       client <---- push ---- server (whenever comment added)
```

### Q3. What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL, and how does DataLoader solve it?
**Answer:** The N+1 problem arises because GraphQL resolvers run per-field. If a query asks for `user(id:42) { posts { author { name } } }` and the `Post.author` resolver naively calls `db.find_author(post.author_id)` for each post, you get 1 query for the user + 1 query for the posts + N queries for the authors = N+2 total. At N=50 posts this is 52 queries; at Facebook's scale this killed databases. **DataLoader** solves it by batching: the `Post.author` resolver does not call the DB directly, it calls `authorLoader.load(post.author_id)`. The loader collects all the IDs requested during a single tick of the event loop (a few milliseconds) and issues ONE batched query: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN (12, 12, 88, ...)`. Each `load()` call returns a promise that resolves when the batch completes. The result: instead of N+2 queries, you get 3 queries (users, posts, batched authors) regardless of N. The trade-off: batching introduces one tick of latency (typically <1 ms), but reduces DB load by orders of magnitude. DataLoader also caches: if two posts have the same `author_id`, the loader returns the cached user instead of refetching. Every production GraphQL server (Apollo Server, GraphQL-Java, Hot Chocolate, Graphene) ships with DataLoader support; it is considered mandatory for any resolver that touches a database or downstream service.
**Visual:**
```
Naive (N+1):                           With DataLoader (3 queries):
user resolver     -> 1 query           user resolver     -> 1 query
posts resolver    -> 1 query           posts resolver    -> 1 query
post1.author      -> 1 query  \        post1.author.load(12)  |
post2.author      -> 1 query   | N     post2.author.load(12)  | tick ends
post3.author      -> 1 query  /        post3.author.load(88)  |
                                       -> 1 batched query: SELECT * FROM users
                                                             WHERE id IN (12,88)
total: N+2 queries                     total: 3 queries (constant, not N+2)
```

### Q4. How does GraphQL caching differ from REST caching?
**Answer:** REST benefits from HTTP caching because each resource has a unique URL — `GET /users/42` can be cached at the CDN, browser, or reverse proxy using `Cache-Control` and `ETag`. GraphQL sends every request to `POST /graphql` with the query in the body, which is not cacheable by HTTP infrastructure (POST responses are never cached by default). Three solutions. (1) **Persisted queries** — the client sends a query ID instead of the full query text: `GET /graphql?id=abc123`. The server looks up the query text by ID (stored at build time), executes it, and the GET response is cacheable by the CDN. Apollo and Relay both support this; GitHub's GraphQL API uses it. (2) **Apollo Client's normalized cache** — on the client side, Apollo normalizes the response into entities keyed by `__typename:id` (e.g., `User:42`); subsequent queries that touch the same entity are served from cache without a network request. This deduplicates across screens: if the home screen fetched user 42's name, the profile screen can read it from cache without re-fetching. (3) **Edge execution** — Cloudflare Workers and similar edge platforms can run GraphQL resolvers at the edge, with edge caching of resolver results. The trade-off: GraphQL caching is more powerful (entity-level deduplication) but more complex than REST's URL-based caching. Stripe deliberately stayed with REST partly because their caching infrastructure (Cloudflare, Fastly) was tuned for URL-keyed REST responses.
**Visual:**
```
REST cache (HTTP-level, URL-keyed):
   GET /users/42 -> Cache-Control: max-age=60 -> CDN cache (1 entry per URL)

GraphQL cache (entity-level, requires work):
   1. Persisted queries: GET /graphql?id=abc -> CDN cacheable
   2. Apollo normalized cache: { User:42 -> {name,avatar}, Post:101 -> {...} }
      subsequent queries touching User:42 served from client cache
   3. Edge execution: Cloudflare Worker runs resolvers, caches results
```

### Q5. What is schema stitching and federation, and when would you use them?
**Answer:** As an organization grows, a single GraphQL schema becomes unwmanageable — hundreds of types, thousands of fields, dozens of teams stepping on each other. Two approaches split the schema across teams. **Schema stitching** (older, mostly superseded): multiple teams run their own GraphQL servers, each with its own schema; a "gateway" server stitches them together by merging types and resolving cross-schema references. The gateway calls each backend, merges the responses, and returns one response to the client. Limitation: merging types across teams is fragile (conflicts on field types, resolvers, naming). **Federation** (Apollo's solution, now the standard): each team runs a service that "owns" certain types and contributes a slice of the schema; a gateway composes the slices into a unified schema. The key innovation: types can be **extended** — the User type might be defined by the `accounts` service (with `id`, `name`, `email`) and extended by the `reviews` service (adding `reviews: [Review]!`). The gateway routes each field resolution to the owning service. This is how Netflix, Spotify, Airbnb, and Wayfair structure their GraphQL: one federated gateway in front of dozens of team-owned services. Trade-offs: federation adds a network hop (client -> gateway -> service), and the gateway is a single point of failure (mitigate with HA deployment and aggressive caching of the composed schema). Federation is the right choice above ~20 backend teams; below that a monolithic schema is simpler.
**Visual:**
```
Federated gateway:
   client --> [gateway]
                |--- resolves User.name/email    -> accounts service
                |--- resolves User.reviews        -> reviews service
                |--- resolves User.orders         -> orders service

Each service contributes a slice:
   accounts:  type User @key(fields:"id") { id name email }
   reviews:   extend type User @key(fields:"id") { id reviews: [Review] }
   orders:    extend type User @key(fields:"id") { id orders: [Order] }
```

### Q6. Why does GraphQL always return HTTP 200 even on errors, and how do you monitor it?
**Answer:** The GraphQL spec says the response is always HTTP 200 OK (assuming the server successfully parsed and started executing the query); errors are reported in the response body's `errors` array: `{ "data": null, "errors": [{ "message": "User not found", "path": ["user"], "extensions": {"code": "NOT_FOUND"} }] }`. The rationale: a single GraphQL query can resolve some fields successfully and others with errors (partial results), so HTTP status cannot capture the full picture. The trade-off: this breaks traditional monitoring that keys on HTTP status — your 5xx alert won't fire on GraphQL errors. Solutions: (1) instrument at the response-body level — parse the `errors` array and emit metrics per error code; Apollo Studio and Datadog's GraphQL integration do this. (2) Add an `extensions` map to each error with a `code` field (`NOT_FOUND`, `UNAUTHORIZED`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`) so dashboards can group by code. (3) For partial failures, return both `data` (with nulls where errors occurred) and `errors` — clients handle partial data gracefully. (4) For auth failures, some teams deviate from the spec and return HTTP 401/403 anyway (HTTP status for transport-level concerns, GraphQL errors for application-level concerns) — this is a pragmatic compromise. Stripe stayed with REST partly because their monitoring and alerting was deeply tied to HTTP status codes, and migrating to GraphQL would have required re-instrumenting everything.
**Visual:**
```
REST:    GET /users/999 -> HTTP 404 (monitor keys on HTTP status)
GraphQL: POST /graphql  -> HTTP 200 (always!)
                            body: { "data": null,
                                    "errors": [{"message":"User not found",
                                                "extensions":{"code":"NOT_FOUND"}}] }
                            monitor must parse body and alert on errors[].extensions.code
```

### Q7. What are persisted queries, and why are they important for production?
**Answer:** A persisted query is a GraphQL query that is uploaded to the server at build time and assigned a unique ID (typically a hash of the query text). At runtime, the client sends only the ID — `GET /graphql?id=abc123` — instead of the full query text. The server looks up the query by ID and executes it. Three benefits. (1) **Security** — without persisted queries, a malicious client can send arbitrarily complex queries (`{ users { posts { comments { author { posts { ... } } } } } }`) to DoS the server; with persisted queries, only pre-approved queries are accepted. (2) **Caching** — `GET /graphql?id=abc123` is cacheable by CDNs and browsers, unlike `POST /graphql`. (3) **Bandwidth** — the query text is often several KB; sending just the ID saves bytes on mobile networks. Apollo Client and Relay both support automatic persisted queries (APQ): the client first tries `GET /graphql?id=abc`; if the server returns 404 (unknown ID), the client falls back to `POST /graphql` with the full query text and the server caches the ID for next time. GitHub's GraphQL API v4 requires persisted queries for unauthenticated requests, allowing only pre-registered queries from public clients. Trade-off: persisted queries add a build step (the build must extract all queries and upload them); this is a tooling cost but worth it for any production GraphQL API.
**Visual:**
```
Build time:
   client code: const QUERY = gql`user(id:42){ name posts{title} }`
   build tool: hash(QUERY) = "abc123"
               upload "abc123" -> "user(id:42){name posts{title}}" to server

Runtime:
   client: GET /graphql?id=abc123      (small, cacheable, no query text leaked)
   server: lookup "abc123" -> query text -> execute -> 200 OK + Cache-Control: max-age=60
   CDN:    cache the response for GET /graphql?id=abc123
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your mobile app renders a feed of 50 posts, each showing the post body, author name, author avatar, and like count. Under REST this is 6 round-trips. How does GraphQL help, and what's the catch?
**Answer:** With REST the client must call `GET /feed` (returns post IDs), then for each post call `GET /posts/{id}`, `GET /users/{author_id}`, `GET /avatars/{avatar_id}` — 6 round-trips per post × 50 posts = 300 round-trips, or 1 round-trip if you have a `/feed?expand=author,avatar` endpoint (but that over-fetches for clients that don't need all fields). With GraphQL the client sends one query: `query { feed { body author { name avatarUrl } likeCount } }` and gets back exactly the fields it needs in one round-trip. The bandwidth savings on mobile are huge — instead of 300 KB of over-fetched JSON, the client receives 30 KB of exactly what it renders. The catch: (1) the server now has a complex resolver tree that touches the posts table, users table, and avatars — and if you don't use DataLoader for the author/avatar resolution, you'll hit N+1 DB queries (50 queries for authors + 50 for avatars). (2) One slow resolver slows the entire response — if `avatarUrl` requires a CDN lookup that takes 200 ms, the whole feed query waits. (3) Error handling is different: if one avatar fetch fails, GraphQL returns `data: { feed: [{ author: { avatarUrl: null } }], errors: [...] }` — partial data, not a 5xx. (4) Rate limiting is harder — a single GraphQL query can be 10x more expensive than a REST call; you need query-cost analysis (e.g., Apollo's cost analyzer) to limit expensive queries. Facebook and Instagram use exactly this pattern on their mobile feeds.
**Visual:**
```
REST: 6 round-trips per post x 50 posts = 300 round-trips
   /feed -> /posts/{id} -> /users/{author_id} -> /avatars/{avatar_id} ...

GraphQL: 1 round-trip, exact fields
   POST /graphql  { feed { body author{ name avatarUrl } likeCount } }
   -> { data: { feed: [ { body, author: {name, avatarUrl}, likeCount } ] } }

catch: must use DataLoader for author/avatar (else N+1 DB queries)
```

### Q2. You are building a GraphQL API for an e-commerce site. The `Product` type has 30 fields. Some clients (mobile) want only `id, name, price, thumbnail`; others (admin dashboard) want all 30 fields plus `inventory, supplier, margin`. How do you handle this?
**Answer:** This is exactly what GraphQL was designed for — the client picks the fields, so you don't need separate endpoints. Mobile client sends `query { product(id:42){ id name price thumbnailUrl } }` and gets only 4 fields. Admin sends `query { product(id:42){ id name price thumbnailUrl inventory supplier { name } margin } }` and gets all 30. The server has one `Product` type with all 30 fields; the executor only resolves the fields the client requested, so the mobile query never touches the inventory or supplier tables. Design decisions: (1) **Authorization** — the `margin` field is admin-only; the resolver checks the caller's role and returns `null` (or throws an authorization error) for non-admin callers. (2) **Cost analysis** — `inventory` requires a call to the warehouse service; if a malicious client requests all 30 fields for 1000 products, the query cost is huge. Use a query-cost analyzer (Apollo's `costAnalysis` plugin) to assign each field a cost and reject queries whose total cost exceeds a limit. (3) **Resolver-level caching** — `thumbnailUrl` is computed once per product; cache it in the request context. (4) **Field deprecation** — when you rename a field, mark the old one `@deprecated(reason: "use thumbnailUrl")` and keep it working for 6+ months. Shopify's storefront API uses exactly this pattern — one Product type, mobile and admin clients each request what they need. Trade-off: the schema becomes the single source of truth and requires governance to avoid field bloat.
**Visual:**
```
type Product {
   id: ID!
   name: String!
   price: Int!
   thumbnailUrl: String
   inventory: Int             @auth(requires: ADMIN)
   supplier: Supplier         @auth(requires: ADMIN)
   margin: Int                @auth(requires: ADMIN)
   ... 30 total fields
}

mobile:   query { product(id:42){ id name price thumbnailUrl } }
admin:    query { product(id:42){ id name price thumbnailUrl inventory supplier{ name } margin } }
```

### Q3. Your GraphQL API has a slow resolver — `Order.shippingTracking` calls an external carrier API (FedEx) that takes 2 seconds. How do you prevent this from slowing down every order query?
**Answer:** Three layers of mitigation. (1) **Field-level deferral** — by default GraphQL resolves all requested fields in parallel and returns the response when all are done; if `shippingTracking` is in the query, the whole response waits 2 seconds. Solution: use the `@defer` directive (GraphQL 2023 spec) to stream the slow field after the rest of the response: the client gets the order data immediately, then receives a patch with `shippingTracking` when it resolves. This requires HTTP streaming or chunked multipart responses. (2) **Caching** — FedEx tracking data changes rarely (every few hours); cache the resolver result in Redis with a 1-hour TTL and a stale-while-revalidate policy so the cache serves even during a FedEx outage. (3) **Field-level timeout** — wrap the FedEx call in a 500 ms timeout; if it exceeds, return `null` for `shippingTracking` and log the timeout — clients should gracefully handle a null tracking field. (4) **Avoid the call entirely** — if the order has not shipped yet (status != SHIPPED), the resolver returns `null` without calling FedEx. (5) **Move to a separate query** — `shippingTracking` becomes a separate `query { shippingTracking(orderId:42){...} }` that the client calls only when the user expands the tracking section, not on every order list render. GitHub uses similar patterns: `Repository.dependencyGraphManifests` is a separate query because it is slow and rarely needed.
**Visual:**
```
Slow query (waits 2s):
   query { order(id:1){ id total shippingTracking { status eta } } }
   -> waits for FedEx call -> 2.0s total

With @defer:
   query { order(id:1){ id total ... @defer shippingTracking { status eta } } }
   -> initial response: { id, total }                       (50ms)
   -> patch: { shippingTracking: { status, eta } }          (2s later, streamed)

Plus: cache FedEx result in Redis (1h TTL) -> 2nd request served in 5ms
```

### Q4. You have 30 backend microservices and want a unified GraphQL API in front of them. Should you build a monolithic GraphQL server or use Apollo Federation?
**Answer:** Above ~5 backend teams, federation is the right choice. A monolithic GraphQL server requires every team to commit to one codebase, coordinate releases, and share an on-call rotation — this scales poorly past a dozen engineers. With federation, each team owns their slice: the `accounts` team owns `type User { id name email }`, the `orders` team owns `extend type User { id orders: [Order] }`, the `reviews` team owns `extend type User { id reviews: [Review] }`. A gateway composes the slices into one schema and routes each field resolution to the owning service. Benefits: (1) teams ship independently — the orders team can deploy a new `Order` field without coordinating with accounts. (2) Clear ownership — every field has an owning team that gets paged when it breaks. (3) Schema governance — the gateway enforces naming conventions, deprecation policies, and breaking-change detection at compose time. Trade-offs: (1) one extra network hop (client -> gateway -> service), adding ~2-5 ms latency. (2) The gateway is a critical piece of infrastructure — it must be HA, autoscaling, and have aggressive caching of the composed schema. (3) Cross-service queries (a query that touches 5 services) require careful tracing to localize failures. Netflix, Airbnb, Spotify, and Wayfair all run federated GraphQL in production with dozens of team-owned subgraphs. Below 5 teams, a monolith is simpler.
**Visual:**
```
Monolithic (small org, <5 teams):
   client -> [one big GraphQL server] -> many DBs

Federated (large org, >5 teams):
   client -> [gateway] -> accounts subgraph  (owns User.name/email)
                      -> orders subgraph     (extends User.orders)
                      -> reviews subgraph    (extends User.reviews)
                      -> payments subgraph   (extends Order.payment)
   each team owns their subgraph; gateway composes unified schema
```

### Q5. Your public GraphQL API is being attacked by malicious clients sending deeply nested queries like `{ users { posts { comments { author { posts { comments { ... } } } } } } }` that take 30 seconds each. How do you protect the server?
**Answer:** Multi-layer defense. (1) **Query depth limiting** — reject queries whose nesting depth exceeds a threshold (e.g., 7 levels). The graphql-depth-limit library does this; Apollo Server ships with it. The malicious query above is 8 levels deep and would be rejected. (2) **Query cost analysis** — assign each field a cost (e.g., scalar field = 1, list field = 5, paginated list = cost × first arg) and reject queries whose total cost exceeds a limit (e.g., 1000). Apollo's `costAnalysis` plugin and GitHub's own cost calculator do this; GitHub's limit is 5000 points per query. (3) **Persisted queries** — for unauthenticated clients, only accept pre-registered queries (sent as `GET /graphql?id=abc`); arbitrary query text is rejected entirely. This eliminates the attack surface for public clients. (4) **Rate limiting** — apply per-client rate limits at the gateway, ideally using the token-bucket pattern with cost-weighted tokens (an expensive query costs more tokens). (5) **Timeout** — wrap query execution in a 5-second timeout; if it exceeds, return an error. (6) **Introspection disable** — in production, disable introspection (`__schema`) so attackers cannot discover your schema to craft malicious queries. (7) **Query allow-listing** — for internal clients, maintain an allow-list of approved queries and reject anything else. GitHub, Shopify, and Facebook all use most of these in production. Trade-off: depth limits and cost analysis can reject legitimate but complex queries — tune the limits based on your real query corpus.
**Visual:**
```
Malicious query (depth 8, cost 50,000):
   { users { posts { comments { author { posts { comments { author {...} } } } } } } }

Defenses:
   1. depth limit (max 7)            -> REJECT "query too deep"
   2. cost analysis (max 1000)       -> REJECT "query too expensive"
   3. persisted queries only         -> REJECT "unknown query ID"
   4. rate limit (1000 pts/min)      -> 429 "too many points"
   5. timeout (5s)                   -> 503 "query timeout"
   6. introspection off              -> cannot discover schema to craft attack
```

### Q6. You are migrating a REST API with 100 endpoints to GraphQL. Should you do a big-bang migration or incremental? How?
**Answer:** Incremental, always. Big-bang migrations of 100 endpoints are high-risk and rarely succeed — too much to test, too many clients to update simultaneously. Three incremental strategies. (1) **GraphQL gateway in front of REST** — stand up a GraphQL server whose resolvers call the existing REST endpoints under the hood. Clients can migrate one screen at a time from REST to GraphQL; both APIs run in parallel. This is the lowest-risk path because the REST endpoints are unchanged. Trade-off: you inherit all the REST N+1 problems inside the GraphQL layer until you rewrite resolvers to call DBs directly. (2) **Wrap and replace per domain** — pick one bounded context (e.g., `orders`) and rewrite its resolvers to call the DB directly, bypassing the REST endpoint. Migrate clients to the GraphQL `orders` queries. Once all clients are migrated, decommission the REST `orders` endpoints. Repeat for the next domain. (3) **Strangler pattern** — keep REST as the default; add GraphQL only for new features that benefit most (mobile feed, dashboards with complex joins). Old REST endpoints remain for stable clients that don't need GraphQL's flexibility. GitHub used a variant of this — they shipped GraphQL API v4 alongside REST v3 and ran both for years; some endpoints are still REST-only. Trade-off: dual maintenance cost — you have to keep both APIs' schemas in sync until one is decommissioned. Plan for 12–24 months of dual-running.
**Visual:**
```
Phase 1 (gateway wraps REST):
   client (GraphQL) -> [GraphQL gateway] -> REST endpoints -> DB
   client (REST)    -> REST endpoints -> DB   (unchanged)

Phase 2 (replace per domain):
   client -> [GraphQL gateway] -> orders resolver -> DB directly (rewritten)
                              -> users resolver   -> REST endpoint (still wrapped)

Phase 3 (REST decommissioned):
   client -> [GraphQL server] -> DB
```

### Q7. Your team wants to add real-time notifications (someone commented on your post) to your GraphQL API. How do you design subscriptions?
**Answer:** Use GraphQL subscriptions over WebSocket. The client opens a WebSocket connection to `wss://api.example.com/graphql` and sends a subscription: `subscription { commentAdded(postId:42){ id body author{ name } } }`. The server registers the subscription and pushes updates whenever a comment is added to post 42. The push payload has the same shape as the subscription: `{ "data": { "commentAdded": { "id": 5, "body": "Nice!", "author": { "name": "Ada" } } } }`. Design decisions: (1) **Transport** — WebSocket (graphql-ws protocol) is the standard; Server-Sent Events (SSE) works for one-directional pushes but does not support client-initiated unsubscribe well. (2) **Pub/sub backbone** — the server subscribes to a message bus (Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka, NATS) for the events; when a comment is added, the comment service publishes to `comment.added.post.42` and every GraphQL server instance subscribed to that topic pushes to its connected clients. (3) **Sticky load balancing** — the WebSocket connection is stateful, so the load balancer must route the same client to the same server (use IP-hash or a session cookie). When that server dies, the client must reconnect and re-subscribe — handle this in the client SDK. (4) **Authorization** — re-check authorization on every push; a user who lost access to post 42 between subscription and push should not receive the update. (5) **Backpressure** — if a client is slow to consume pushes, the server should buffer up to N messages then drop the subscription (do not let memory grow unbounded). (6) **Scaling** — at 1M concurrent subscriptions, you need many GraphQL servers each holding a subset of connections, plus a scalable pub/sub backbone. Netflix and GitHub use subscriptions for live studio notifications and issue updates.
**Visual:**
```
client --WebSocket--> graphql server --subscribe--> Redis Pub/Sub
                                       (topic: comment.added.post.42)

comment service -> publishes to Redis -> graphql server pushes to client:
   { "data": { "commentAdded": { "id": 5, "body": "Nice!",
                                  "author": { "name": "Ada" } } } }

scaling: 1M concurrent subs across N graphql servers, each holding ~100k conns
         sticky LB routes same client to same server (stateful WS)
         on server death, client reconnects + re-subscribes (client SDK handles)
```

quiz.explanation: The N+1 problem arises because GraphQL resolvers run per-field. If a query asks for user(id:42) { posts { author { name } } } and the Post.author resolver naively calls db.find_author(post.author_id) for each post, you get 1 query for the user + 1 query for the posts + N queries for the authors = N+2 total. At N=50 posts this is 52 queries; at Facebook's scale this killed databases.

quiz.explanation: Schema stitching** (older, mostly superseded): multiple teams run their own GraphQL servers, each with its own schema; a "gateway" server stitches them together by merging types and resolving cross-schema references. The gateway calls each backend, merges the responses, and returns one response to the client. Limitation: merging types across teams is fragile (conflicts on field types, resolvers, naming).
